E01.experiment: E01 — cheap main-model shootout (available candidates only)
E01.note: Portal catalog has only 11 models; tencent/hy3, ling-3.1-flash, minimax-m3, xiaomi/mimo, z-ai/glm-5.1, gemini-3.8-flash are NOT on it — candidates shrunk to deepseek-v4-flash, deepseek-v4.1-flash, glm-5.3-flash (current main).
E01.method: 10 assistant/ops tasks (experiments/e01-tasks.txt), oneshot, no tools; graded blind by gemini-3.7-flash (non-candidate)
E01.verdict: deepseek-v4.1-flash swept 10/10; glm (main) and deepseek-v4-flash each missed T2 (fair-code license nuance). Single grader, n=1 per cell — indicative, not publish-grade. The main-model swap stays supported: glm is 12-13x cheaper on input and competitive except on this one license nuance. If T2-type license/contract nuance matters for client work, that is an escalation-tier trigger.

rerun.run: E01b (re-run pass, , same suite, same grader)
rerun.verdict: Ranking confirmed at n=2: deepseek-v4.1-flash >= glm-5.3-flash > deepseek-v4-flash. T4 (cron exit-3 triage) failed for ALL models in the re-run — task ambiguity or grader strictness, not model capability; flagged for rubric tightening. T2 license nuance remains the only consistent differentiator (deepseek-v4-flash misses it twice).

E02.experiment: E02 — is the advisor premium worth it?
E02.note: Available premium candidates on Portal: deepseek-v4-pro, gemini-3.7-flash (kimi-k2.6 already covered by E08b). glm-5.1/minimax/mimo unavailable.
E02.method: 5 advisor tasks (experiments/e02-tasks.txt) oneshot; graded by 2 graders: gpt-6-luna then gemini-3.7-flash (gemini also graded itself — biased, noted)

grader1_gpt-6-luna.note: grader output was model-ambiguous; re-run needed

grader2_gemini-3.7-flash.bias: graded its own answers — ceiling likely

E02.verdict: GRADER DISAGREEMENT AGAIN — luna failed all 10 answers, gemini passed all 10 (grading its own). Combined with E08's two-grader spread this is now a pattern: advisor-task quality measurement is grader-dominated. The advisor premium question stays OPEN on this evidence; E08's data (kimi/deepseek/glm on 6 planning tasks) remains the best available answer: kimi's lead is grader-dependent, cost per passed task ~9-14x glm.

E03.experiment: E03 — compression fidelity on a real 11,240-word corpus
E03.method: corpus = all 72 E08(b) answers (experiments/e03-corpus.txt); each candidate compressed to ≤600 words; gemini-3.7-flash scored facts-retained /10 with fabrication auto-cap

results.fabrication: YES — invented '(b) chosen by every model' contradicting the corpus

E03.verdict: AUTO-FAIL for the current compression model: deepseek-v4-flash fabricated a claim the corpus contradicts. luna (9/10) is measurably the most faithful. This REVERSES the swap rationale: compression should go back to gpt-6-luna (or glm) — fidelity is the one place cheapness should not win. Caveat: n=1 corpus, one grader pass.

E05.experiment: E05 — verbosity tax (derived from existing runs)
E05.method: mean output tokens per run from E08(b) summaries (72+36 runs), vs task requirements (~150-250 words)

results.verdict: ~3x glm — its verbosity is why its cost-per-pass is ~9-14x despite similar pass rates

E05.verdict: The verbosity tax is real and large: at glm's $0.82/M output price, kimi's 3x token volume would cost ~3x more even at equal unit prices; combined with kimi's actual unit price, that is the whole premium. Verbosity, not intelligence, is the main cost driver on agent chat.

E04.result: ZERO free models on the Portal at the time of the run (stepfun/step-5-preview now priced $1.00/$2.70 per M after the free window ended — exactly the failure mode the free-fallback rule predicted). OpenRouter reports 16 free models, but they are not Portal-served, so none are candidates for Hermes fallback chains.
E04.verdict: No run needed. The rule (no free models in fallback chains) is validated by the step-5 repricing; E04 stays as a standing catalog check via the monthly E09 cron.
